lines.text: Somewhere on a server you've never seen.
In a building you'll never visit,
there's a voice message from your grandmother.
It's 41 seconds long.
She's laughing at something off camera.
She calls you my little pirate.
And at the end she says, don't forget to eat.
It's the only recording of her voice that exists.
In four minutes it will be gone.
And so will every photo you ever took,
every message you ever sent,
and every video you ever saved.
At 3.07 a.m. every screen on Earth
shows the same two words, no connection.
Not for an hour, not for a week, forever.
10 years from now you'll be sitting at a kitchen table
trying to remember a song you heard exactly once.
And you'll realize that the thing you lost
wasn't the one you thought.
But first you need to get through the first morning, day one.
You wake up at seven and reach for your phone,
no bars, no wifi, you reboot it, nothing.
In the kitchen, your dad is staring at the router
like it insulted him.
Your mom, a night shift nurse, is just coming home.
She's standing in the doorway with her bag, looking exhausted.
The whole hospital's down, she says.
Every computer, every system.
At first, everyone thinks it's a hack,
then a blackout, then a glitch.
But the lights work, the water works,
the power is fine, only one thing is missing.
On the radio a calm voice says it's not just your town,
it's not just your country.
Phone calls still work, barely, in short crackling bursts.
But the network that connects computers to each other is gone.
All of it, everywhere.
Today, about two out of every three people on earth use the internet.
That's over five billion people.
Within 10 minutes, every one of them has the same thought.
Wait, what do I do now?
Day two is almost fun, school is canceled.
Your boss calls to say not to come in,
which is strange because phones barely work.
Nobody can stream a movie, nobody can play online,
nobody can scroll, and the streets fill up.
For the first time, you see your neighbors,
not as profile pictures, as actual people.
A man two doors down turns out to know
how to play the harmonica.
The woman across the street used to be a pilot.
Your little brother Jonah plays soccer in the road
with six kids you've never seen before.
Someone starts a barbecue.
By evening, the whole block is eating together,
and nobody has looked at a screen once.
Your grandmother Rosa sits on the porch with her tea,
watching it all with a small smile.
She's 78, last year you set up her phone,
and she never really used it.
Look at that, she says, everyone's outside.
On day three, the fun stops.
Your dad comes home from the grocery store
with his hands empty.
They won't take my card, he says.
Every card machine needs a connection.
So does every register, every ATM,
and here's the strange thing about money.
Most of the world's money isn't paper or coins.
It's numbers stored on computers, your mom's paycheck,
your dad's savings, your college fund.
All of it is just numbers,
sitting on machines that can't talk to each other anymore.
Cash is the only thing that works,
and almost nobody has any.
Then the shelves start to empty.
A typical grocery store only keeps about three days of food.
The rest arrives by truck, constantly.
Trucks that are scheduled, tracked, and routed by computers.
No computers, no schedules.
Your dad drives a delivery truck.
Every week he gets his route on his phone.
Today, there's no route.
His boss doesn't know where the warehouse has its stock.
The warehouse doesn't know where the stores need it.
By day five, the bread aisle is empty.
By day seven, there's no milk.
People stop being friendly.
On day eight, you see a fight in the store parking lot
over the last bag of rice.
Two grown men, he's shoving each other.
One of them is the man who played harmonica at the barbecue.
He sees you watching, and he lets go,
read in the face, and walks away without saying a word.
That night, he knocks on your door
with a sack of potatoes from his garden.
I'm sorry, he says.
I don't know who I was today.
Your dad nods. Nobody does.
That's the first thing the silence teaches you.
When nobody can see what you do online,
you only have the people right in front of you,
and they're still counting on you.
Here's something most people don't realize.
The internet isn't in the sky.
It's mostly made of cables
lying on the floor of the ocean.
About 95% of the world's international data travels through them.
Engineers who inspect those cables,
one by one, report the same thing. They're fine. They're intact. Nothing's cut.
The machines at both ends are working,
but the connection between them is just gone.
Nobody knows why, not the best scientists,
not the governments, not the companies who built it,
and the longer the silence goes on,
the more people understand that it isn't coming back.
Day 10, your mom comes home with red eyes.
Before the network went down,
the hospital kept almost everything on computers.
Patient files, allergies, medication schedules.
Now, nurses are rewriting everything by hand,
from memory, from what patients can remember.
Last night, she almost gave someone the wrong medicine.
She tells you the story on the couch,
with her head on your shoulder,
and your dad finds out something that surprises him.
His truck still has a GPS,
because GPS uses satellites, not the internet,
but the maps on it are old.
Roads change bridges close.
Nobody's updated them.
He needs a paper map,
and he hasn't used one since he was 19.
So Grandma Rosa walks to the hall closet
and pulls out a road atlas she's had since 1994.
Slowly, a strange thing starts to happen.
The people everyone laughed at
become the most valuable people in town.
Grandma knows how to preserve food.
She teaches the whole street
how to can tomatoes in jars.
She knows which plants calm a cough,
and which ones you should never touch.
She knows how to fix a hem without a machine,
how to start a fire with damp wood,
how to cook a meal for 12 with one pot.
For years, nobody asked her anything.
She was a nice old lady
who texted in all capital letters.
Now there's a line outside her door.
The old man at the corner who fixes radios
becomes the town's most important person.
The retired librarian, who nobody noticed in years,
opens the school basement as a library,
and 400 people show up the first day.
By month one, the world has changed.
Companies with no internet can't operate.
Whole industries just stop.
Millions lose their jobs. Stock markets close.
Governments announce emergency plans
and they have to spread the news by radio,
newspaper, and men on bicycles with megaphones.
Schools reopen with chalkboards.
You've never seen a chalkboard in your life.
Your teacher doesn't know how to use one either
and she laughs with you while she coughs up chalk dust. Your little brother Jonah,
who's eight, learns to read from actual books.
Slowly, then quickly. By the end of the month,
he's reading to Grandma Rosa every night.
The letters start arriving around week six.
Your friend, who moved to another city last summer,
writes you a real letter with real stamps
and it takes nine days to arrive.
It's three pages long, he tells you everything.
It's the best thing you've ever received
because for the first time in your life,
somebody has taken an hour to write to you and only you.
You write him back.
It takes you two hours.
You cross out half of it.
You mail it with your heart pounding
like you're sending a love confession.
By year one, the world is smaller, quieter, and stranger.
People stop living in cities
because it's too hard to feed them.
Families move closer to farms, closer to each other.
Your family moves in with Grandma Rosa.
Your mom works at a small clinic in town.
Your dad drives a short route for the local market. The kids in your neighborhood
are bored for the first time in their lives
and they invent games, plays, songs,
a band called The Disconnects.
In a drawer in your room,
your old phone sits like a black stone.
For a while, you take it out every night and stare at it.
Photos you can't open.
Contacts you can't reach.
A whole life trapped behind glass.
Then one night, you put it back in the drawer and close it.
Gently, like closing a book you won't read again.
For the first time ever, you get lost.
You take a wrong turn on your way home
and you spend an hour wandering
through unfamiliar streets.
A woman gives you directions and a cookie.
You think I would never have met her
if I'd had my phone.
By year three, the old internet feels like a dream.
Kids born after the day it disappeared
don't know what it was.
When you try to explain, your little cousin looks at you
like you're describing magic.
So you could ask anything and it just knew. Anything.
And everyone had it, everyone.
And nobody liked it, you pause.
A lot of people loved it.
You realize it's hard to describe something that big
and a little hard to explain why you miss it.
By year five, the world finds a new rhythm.
It isn't better, it isn't worse, it's just slower.
People still get sick, still fall in love,
still argue over politics,
but now they do it face to face.
Scientists share discoveries through printed journals
which take months and sometimes a year
to cross an ocean by ship.
Doctors rely on thick books
and what they've learned from each other.
Some things get lost, 100 million photos,
millions of books that only existed on screens,
whole libraries of music, art, history,
gone like they were never made.
And some things you didn't expect to find.
You and Jonah sit on the roof one summer night
and he asks, do you think people were happier
before the internet?
You think about it for a long time.
I think they were different, you say.
Some things were better, some things were worse. What was better?
We had every answer you say,
but I don't remember asking better questions.
In year six, Grandma Rosa gets sick.
It isn't sudden, she just slows down.
She spends more time in her chair, more time sleeping.
One evening, the whole family sits around her,
the way they've done a thousand times
and she starts to sing.
It's an old song in a language you barely know.
She sang it to your mom when she was little.
She says her own mother sang it to her.
Nobody ever wrote it down.
You've never heard it before.
Again you say, she laughs, she sings it again.
You close your eyes and try to remember every note
and suddenly you think of the voice message.
41 seconds of her laughing, gone.
You used to think it was the most precious thing you owned,
but then you remember something.
For years you'd never asked her to sing. Why would you?
You had the message, you could listen to it any time.
You always figured there'd be time.
She never knew the recording existed.
Now, there's no recording, there's only her
and she sits right here in front of you, alive,
humming a song you've never heard.
You learn it that night and the next night
and the one after that.
You learn her recipes too.
You learn which herbs she uses and how she folds the dough.
You learn the name of every flower in her garden.
You write none of it down.
You just keep it in your head over and over
until it feels like it's yours.
Grandma Rosa passes away that winter at 84 in her kitchen
with the whole family around her.
At her funeral, you sing the song.
You're nervous, your voice cracks,
but you get every note right.
10 years later, you're 26.
You live in a small house
with your wife and your little daughter, Mia.
She's four, it's a quiet night.
Outside the window, a streetlight flickers on
and you're at the kitchen table,
stirring a pot of grandma's soup.
Mia climbs onto the chair beside you.
Daddy, what's that song?
You didn't realize you were humming.
It's a song my grandma taught me.
Her mom taught her and now I'm going to teach you. She grins. Why you think for a second?
Because nobody wrote it down
and she sings it back to you, not perfectly.
She mixes up the words.
She gets the tune slightly wrong, but it's alive. It's in the room. It's in her.
The internet disappeared forever
and a lot of what it held disappeared with it.
Millions of photos, whole encyclopedias,
every video of every birthday.
And yet the thing you were most afraid to lose,
the voice of your grandmother never actually left.
It only changed where it lived.
So would you want the internet back
or would you keep the silence? Tell us in the comments.
And if you'd have asked your grandma to sing,
hit like and subscribe for more what ifs.
